title: Please Don't Throw Me in the Briar Patch
text:
These tales come from the African American storytelling of the South, written down and published by Joel Chandler Harris in 1880.

Brer Fox was tired of being outwitted by Brer Rabbit, so he made a figure out of tar, dressed it, and set it by the road. Brer Rabbit came along and greeted it politely. The tar baby said nothing. Offended, Brer Rabbit hit it, and his fist stuck. He hit it with the other fist, kicked it and butted it, until he was stuck fast all over. Then Brer Fox strolled out from the bushes, laughing.

Now Brer Fox debated aloud how to finish him off. He might roast him over a fire, hang him or drown him. Brer Rabbit said he did not care what Brer Fox did to him, so long as he did not throw him into the briar patch. Roast me, he said, hang me, drown me, skin me, but please, please do not fling me into that briar patch.

Brer Fox wanted to hurt Brer Rabbit as much as possible, so he grabbed him by the hind legs and threw him right into the middle of the thorns. There was a moment of silence. Then, from a log on the hill, Brer Rabbit called down that he had been born and raised in a briar patch, and skipped away.
lesson: When you are in a weak position, your opponent's eagerness to hurt you can become your exit. Think about what they believe you fear, and use it.
location: Southern United States (African American folk tradition)
source: Joel Chandler Harris, Uncle Remus: His Songs and His Sayings (1880), The Wonderful Tar-Baby Story and How Mr. Rabbit Was Too Sharp for Mr. Fox
